name: Agreement of June 23, 1875 by the Sioux relinquishing hunting privileges in Nebraska
nations: Lakota, Dakota and Nakota (Oceti Sakowin) of the Great Sioux Reservation
Oglala Sioux Tribe (listed by OSU as successor in interest)
promises: The Sioux gave up the hunting privilege guaranteed by Article 11 of the 1868 treaty and their right to the part of the Article 16 unceded country lying in Nebraska (Royce schedule).
No payment or other return is stated in the sources opened (see openQuestions).
landTaken: Royce Area 584, which Royce notes overlaps the Pawnee cession of September 24, 1857.
today: No court, Claims Commission or government finding about this agreement was located. The Commission's 1970 opinion in Docket 74 on Articles 11 and 16 of the 1868 treaty treats the hunting rights as part of the 1868 valuation and does not mention the 1875 agreement. The 1868 treaty and the 1877 Act are recorded under kappler-1006 and cession-1876-09-26-arapaho-northern-cheyenne-sioux.

openQuestions: Oklahoma State University tags the agreement 'Not Ratified' and gives no Statutes at Large citation; Royce lists it as an agreement. Its ratification status is unsettled.

A 19th-century Commissioner of Indian Affairs report, seen only as a search snippet, says the Sioux surrendered the privilege for $25,000 appropriated by Congress; that report was not opened, so the sum is not recorded as fact.
Whether the agreement had the consent of three-fourths of adult Sioux men, which Article 12 of the 1868 treaty required for any cession, was not found.
Audit 2026-11-08: the second promise said the United States was to pay a sum Congress had appropriated; neither Royce nor the OSU record says so, so it was replaced.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's history says Article 11 of the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty kept for the Great Sioux Nation hunting rights over a far larger area than the reservation, south to the Republican and Platte rivers, that no cession was valid without three-fourths of the adult men, and that it holds its 1851 and 1868 treaty rights as binding today as when they were made.
